Uniform Title: Kṣurikopaniṣat Main Title: Yoga Upaniṣads with the Commentary of Śrī Upaniṣadbrahmayogin Secondary Title: Kṣurikopaniṣat
Commentator: Brahmayogin (also known as Śrī Upaniṣad Brahmayogin) Editor: Śāstrī Mahādeva

The Kṣurikopaniṣad. "May He protect us both"—thus the peace invocation. The Section on Yoga.
I shall fully explain the *kṣurikā* concentration for the sake of attaining success in yoga;
having attained which, rebirth no longer occurs for one joined in yoga.
This exposition, ordained according to the true meaning of the Vedas as spoken by the Self-Existent One himself,
is the excellent seat upon the supreme ground situated within the channel of liberation (*kaivalya-nāḍikā*).
I take refuge in Rāma, who shines with the yoga of the Kṣurikopaniṣad.

Indeed, this *Kṣurikopaniṣad*, belonging to the Black Yajurveda, has been set forth as a treatise on yoga (*yogaśāstra*) for the purpose of dispelling the obstacles to knowledge. Its introductory section and other formalities are to be inferred from the *Kaṭhavallī*. A commentary on this work, characterized by the aforementioned definitions, is now begun from its brief text. The fact that the Śruti itself proceeds spontaneously, addressing those who possess the qualifications already described, is for the sake of praising that knowledge. To the question "What is this Śruti?", it says: "The Razor" (*kṣurikām*). For those who are endowed with the aforementioned means of yoga, I shall correctly expound the "Razor"—a form of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) resembling a weapon, which is as sharp as a razor at cutting the knot of the heart consisting of one's own ignorance, and characterized by the contemplation that "nothing exists apart from Brahman. For what purpose? For the constant contemplation of Brahman alone.

(37) *Yoga* means that which leads to its attainment—that is, for the sake of realizing it. Having attained that concentration (*dhāraṇā*) characterized by the aforementioned definition, for the sage who is united in yoga, there is no further birth; that is, the cycle of birth and death does not occur. "I shall fully explain that very [concentration]"—this is the connection with what precedes. (1) What is the definition of that yoga? By whom was it taught? What is the collection of its means? To this he says: "Veda... It is that which is established by the Supreme Lord, the Self-born (*svayaṃbhū*), as taught to Brahmā in the *Yogaśikhā* and other scriptures; the meaning is that it is ordained according to the true meaning of the Vedas and is in agreement with all the Upaniṣads.
Having resorted to a noiseless place for the postures and breath control, he remains there established in his seat.
Having withdrawn the limbs like a tortoise and restrained the mind within the heart,
one should [practice] gradually by means of the Praṇava through the yoga of twelve measures.
One should fill the entire self while blocking all the apertures; [holding] the chest, face, hips, and neck [steady], with the heart slightly raised. (4)
One should cause the vital breaths moving within the nostrils to enter that [state];
having become one whose breath is extended therein, one should slowly exhale.

He teaches the means for the attainment of such yoga, beginning with the word "soundless" (*niḥśabdam*). One who seeks the state of non-conceptual yoga (*nirvikalpaka-yoga*) should resort to a soundless place, free from the crowding of people; staying there in a secluded spot, he should assume a perfected posture such as the lotus-posture (*padmāsana*). (2) Having withdrawn the senses, beginning with hearing, like a tortoise its limbs, and having restrained the mind within his own heart—the word "and" (*ca*) indicating that he should make the mind free from the volitions that serve as the gateway for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the senses—he should circumambulate his knees, neither too quickly nor too slowly.
One should snap the fingers; that is proclaimed as one *mātrā*.

(As stated on p. 38: By means of the *praṇava* consisting of four *mātrās*—joined with twelve *mātrās* representing the nature of time established by the *Śruti*—one should very gradually fill one’s entire self or one’s own body with air. Regarding how the retention of air (*vāyudhāraṇā*) can be achieved when there are openings for the exit of air: [the text says] "having blocked all the gates," such as the *apāna* and others. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that one should hold the filled air for a duration of forty-eight *mātrās*. Having performed the retention (*dhāraṇā*) in this manner, he states that one should exhale (*recayet*) correctly: "chest... (verse 4). The yogi, established in a perfected posture (*āsana*), [should consider] "chest, mouth, waist, and neck"—that is, *uro-mukha-kaṭi-grīvam*. Because these are parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), they form a singular compound. Having made the heart slightly elevated... (verse 4). Having thus held the breath for the aforementioned duration, one should exhale very gradually; that is, one should release the air filled for twenty-four *mātrās*. Having filled the air through the *iḍā* and retained it, one should exhale through the *piṅgalā*; then, having again filled it through the *piṅgalā* and retained it, one should exhale through the *iḍā*. The sense is that one should perform eighty *prāṇāyāmas* in this way, four times every day. (Verse 5)
Having made oneself steady and firm through withdrawal (pratyāhāra), one who is composed should place the [toes] with the big toes;
one should apply two at the ankles and three each on the calves. (6)
There are two knees and likewise two thighs; three [joints] in the anus and three in the penis.
One should take refuge in the region of the navel, which is the locus of the anus.
Therein, the channel Suṣumnā is indeed surrounded by ten channels;
there [are those that are] red, yellow, black, copper-colored, and deep red.
One should resort to the channel that is exceedingly subtle, thin, and white;
there one should cause the vital breaths to circulate, as a spider does with its thread.
(39) Then, that great abode of the heart, shining like a red lotus, that small *puṇḍarīka* is what is described in the Vedāntas. (10)
Having pierced that, it reaches the throat; one should fill that channel.

Having described the characteristics of posture (*āsana*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he states the characteristic of withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) with the word "firmly" (*sthiram*). Thus, through proficiency in the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, the yogi, having assumed the perfected *padmāsana* or another posture, and having become one whose senses are concentrated, should block the nostrils with the thumbs along with the ring and little fingers. Having made his own self, mind, and vital breath firm so that they remain steady in the heart, and having maintained the pure *kumbhaka* (retention of breath), he should then perform *dhāraṇā* (concentration) by directing the vital air into the two ankles. By the word "tu" (but/and), it is indicated that he should also direct the air into the toes of the feet. Then, regarding the calves and the regions of the calves, the repetition "three by three" is for the sake of emphasis. The nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative: "three by three" refers to the eyes, mind, and vital breath; having directed these three in sequence into the toes, ankles, and calves, he should withdraw them from each respective place. (6) Likewise, he should withdraw the eyes, mind, and vital breath—three by three—from the two knees, the two thighs, the anus, and the penis. Having performed *kumbhaka* and withdrawn them from the knees, thighs, *mūlādhāra*, and *svādhiṣṭhāna* respectively, he should then direct the eyes, mind, and vital breath into the region of the navel, the *maṇipūraka*, which is the abode or support of the anus and other centers; there, until mastery is achieved, he should take refuge in that. (7) There, within the bulbous root (*kanda*) of the channel that serves as the support for the *maṇipūraka*, there exists a certain channel of Brahman named *suṣumnā*, surrounded by ten channels such as *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and others. In that very bulbous root of the channels, there are the red, and by the word "ca" (and), the brownish-red (*kapiśā*); the yellow, and by the word "ca", the tawny (*piṅgalā*); the black, the copper-colored, and the deep red. This collection of ten channels, distinguished by colors such as pale-white and so on, includes *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, *gāndhārī*, *varuṇā*, and others. (8) It is subtle and slender. By the two uses of the word "ca," it is indicated that there are seventy-two thousand principal channels. Among all the channels, he should take refuge in that white *suṣumnā* channel, which is preeminent and radiant with a white color. He says "therein" (*tatra*) to indicate that one should withdraw the eyes, mind, and vital breath into it. The meaning is that just as a spider moves along its thread, so should one transfer the eyes and other faculties into the *suṣumnā*. (9) Then, from the path of the *suṣumnā*, [one reaches] the abode of the heart, which has the luster of a red lotus, in relation to the channels.

p. 40) Regarding the "great" [space] and the "small lotus dwelling" mentioned in the Vedānta texts, one should withdraw the three—sight and the others—into that small lotus located within the heart fixed upon the *suṣumnā* channel. (10) Then, having pierced that heart-lotus, sight and the others proceed to the throat and the *viśuddhi-cakra* situated there. Having withdrawn them there, one should then fill—that is, withdraw them into—the *ājñā-cakra* at the midpoint of the eyebrows, and thereafter the *sahasrāra-cakra*. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).
Retention, meditation, and concentration are the supreme secret of the mind— extremely sharp and pure in intellect.
One should constantly contemplate that form which is the vital point (marman) above the foot, relying upon yoga with a sharp flow of the mind. 12.
That which is called the "Indra-vajra" [mudrā] cuts through the vital points and the shanks; one should sever it by means of meditation, breath-control (yoga), and concentrations (dhāraṇās). || 13 ||
Having established [the breath] between the upper [breaths], which releases the vital force from the vital points,
one should, after practicing four times through yoga, cut [the bonds] without hesitation.
Then, within the throat, the yogi should draw together the collection of channels;
among those one hundred and one channels, the supreme one is situated in their midst.
The Suṣumnā is merged in the Supreme, while Virajā is of the nature of Brahman;
Iḍā stands on the left, and Piṅgalā on the right.
He who knows that supreme place situated between those two is a knower of the Veda.
There are seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) in each [channel], according to Taitila.

By means of the yoga of meditation, all [channels] are severed, yet the single *suṣumṇā* is not severed, by that razor which is the stainless essence of yoga and possesses the brilliance of fire. (18)
The wise yogi should sever the hundred channels in this very life from their source;
when he perceives the *taitila* [vital point] as being like a *jātī* flower, [he attains liberation]. 19.
In this way, one should contemplate that channel through auspicious and inauspicious states;
once it has been so cultivated, those [beings] enter it, freed from rebirth.

Next, he describes the characteristics of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* with the words "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*). "Of the mind" means beyond the thousandfold fluctuations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to show that the mind and its effects do not exist in reality. It is "secret" (*guhya*), because it must be concealed from those who lack qualification. It is "very sharp" (*sutīkṣṇa*), because it possesses the weapon of one’s own knowledge, which is as sharp as a blade for cutting the thread of ignorance and its effects. It is "pure-intellect-perceivable" (*buddhinirmala*), because it is to be known by a pure intellect. (11) One should contemplate and hold the thought: "I am that whose form is the vital point (*marman*) above the collection of feet beginning with Viśva, Virāṭ, and Otrā—namely, the limit established by the awakening to the impossibility of Viśva and the rest. He says that such concentration on Brahman (*brahmadhāraṇā*) cuts the knot of one’s own ignorance with the words "the mind" (*manaḥ*). The syntactical connection is: "Thus, constantly and always, with the sharp edge of the mind—one whose nature is the weapon of mental concentration consisting of the thought 'nothing exists apart from Brahman'—one should cut through the delusion of one’s own ignorance. (12) That which is called the "Indra-Vajra" because it shatters the mountain of one’s own ignorance, and which cuts away limbs such as the vital points of what is other than oneself—that kind of yoga characterized by the piercing of the *suṣumnā* should be resorted to. By the power of meditation that "I am that Brahman," and by means of concentrations (*dhāraṇās*) on specific locations from the big toe to the end of the *sahasrāra*, one should sever the delusion of anything other than oneself. (13) If, however, the delusion of something other than oneself arises again, then one should perform *dhāraṇā* by establishing the sight, mind, and breath in that middle state which is free of conceptualization (*avikalpa*) between the two thighs of one’s own ignorance—the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), which are the supports for the superimposition and negation (*āropāpavāda*) of Viśva, Virāṭ, and Otrā, and their respective *turiya* states. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of emphasis. Through the aforementioned yoga, having practiced four times the release of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which is the support for the superimposition and negation of the ignorance-state and its effects, including the four parts starting with the gross (*sthūla*)—and having performed the negation of the four parts starting with the gross along with the vital breath, one should negate the substratum of that negation.

(42) By the power of the mental retention (*dhāraṇā*) "I am Brahman," the yogi, free from doubt, should sever the obstacles to yoga. (14) To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*). Since the perfection of yoga does not occur without the purification of the collection of channels (*nāḍī*), for that reason the yogi should properly direct the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) into the collection of channels shining within his own throat; by means of the method of *kevala-kumbhaka* alone, he should effect the purification of the collection of channels. To the question "Which are the principal channels?", he says: "One" (*ekā*). Within the center of one's own body, there exists a hundred principal channels beginning with *iḍā*, increasing by one. Among them, the stable channel *suṣumnā* is supreme, being the most excellent of all. (15) This very *suṣumnā* is merged in the Supreme Brahman, because it is the "thread of Brahman" (*brahmasūtra*). It is "dustless" (*virajā*), due to the absence of modifications of *rajas* and *tamas*. It is "of the nature of Brahman" (*brahmarūpiṇī*), because it is the cause for attaining the world of Brahman. He states the fruit of knowing the *suṣumnā*: "Iḍā" (*iḍā*). [The third case ending here functions as the locative] on the left side of the *suṣumnā*; that is, *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* abide on the left and right sides of the *suṣumnā*. (16) Between those two, in the *suṣumnā*, exists the supreme, most excellent station of Brahman. The sage who knows that Supreme Self situated there as non-different from his own inner self (*pratyagātman*) becomes a knower of Brahman, the meaning of the Vedas. By the yoga of meditation as described, the movement of the vital air in the channels other than the *suṣumnā* is severed, but the movement of the vital air in the *suṣumnā* is not severed. He says: "Seventy-two" (*dvāsaptati*). There are seventy-two thousand principal channels. Therein, by the yoga of meditation upon the non-dual Consciousness-only (*cinmātra*) situated within the *kaivalya-nāḍikā* inside the *suṣumnā* channel, the characteristic coming and going of the vital air in each individual channel—(17)—is severed, is cut off. At that time, the single *suṣumnā*—the activity of sight, mind, and vital air within the *kaivalya-nāḍikā* in the middle of the *suṣumnā*—is not severed; it does not perish until the end of the Brahma-cycle (*kalpa*), nor does it go outside; at the end of the cycle, it undergoes dissolution into the Formless (*virūpa*). Therefore, the body of the sage whose activities of sight, vital air, and mind have entered the *kaivalya-nāḍī* remains until the end of the Brahma-cycle. On this point, the word of the Blessed Lord is the authority: [The verse continues: "The body of the yogi whose life-force has entered the *kaivalya-nāḍī* remains until the end of the Brahma-cycle, like a lamp in a jar. (18) By the power of the aforementioned yoga, the yogi, having become free from doubt, should sever the obstacles to yoga. (19) Having severed the obstacles to yoga, the yogi, becoming free from doubt, should contemplate the Supreme Brahman which is devoid of all attributes. (20) [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly after the commentary on verse 19.]
At first, the row of organs belonging to the knower of the true self enters the space of consciousness within the channel of liberation;
then, undergoing dissolution up to the Brahma-kalpa, it remains having attained liberation through the body.

Thus, because it is so, the wise yogi—yoga being the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), and such yoga itself being the stainless essence in the form of a subtle stream—with that stainless essence of yoga, which is like a razor possessing the brilliance of fire, should, in this very life through its power, sever the hundred channels along with the movement of the vital breaths within them, [directing them] solely into the channel of liberation (kaivalya-nāḍī). || 18 ||

The sense is that one should effect the movement of sight, mind, and breath [through the *suṣumnā*]. He states—beginning with the word "jāti"—that by means of the movement or non-movement of the winds in the channels (*nāḍī*) leading to liberation (*kaivalya*) and those other than them, the yogi becomes one who has accomplished his purpose. Just as the fragrance of a *jātī* flower is inseparable from the flower itself, when the yogi, endowed with the aforementioned means, perceives the stability of sight, mind, and breath within the channel of liberation (*kaivalyanāḍī*), he then becomes liberated while in the body (*videhamukta*). This is because the lexicon (*kośa*) defines "movement" (*gamana*) as "stability" (*taitila*). Thus, one should contemplate that the movement of sight, mind, and breath through the channels other than the *kaivalyanāḍī* located within the *suṣumnā* is joined with auspicious and inauspicious states characterized by going to and returning from heaven and hell. This *suṣumnā* channel grants the state of non-return (*apunarbhava*); this *kaivalyanāḍī* within the *suṣumnā* grants the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*); the multitude of channels other than that, such as the *ramā*, lead to auspicious results like heaven; the multitude of channels such as the *aramā* lead to inauspicious results like hell; and the other channels lead to various diverse states such as disease. In this regard, the *Śruti* says: "By merit, *ramā* leads to the world of merit; by sin, *aramā* leads to the world of sin; whatever one remembers with desire, that one attains; for the sake of non-rebirth, one pierces the sheath"; and "Death, indeed, becomes one with the supreme deity," and so forth. Since the movement of wind through the other channels is the cause of the auspicious and inauspicious, one should, through the practice of yoga, restrain that movement and contemplate the movement of the wind only within the *suṣumnā* and other [liberating] channels. He states the fruit of such contemplation—beginning with the word "tat": Having thus superimposed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the *suṣumnā* etc., and having contemplated with the thought "I am that Brahman," they, being freed from rebirth by such contemplation, attain that very Brahman. || 20 ||
The practice of yoga and its qualified practitioner:

one who has conquered the mind through austerity, having resorted to a noiseless place, free from attachment, knowing the limbs of yoga, and being indifferent to worldly concerns, [should practice] gradually and steadily. (21)

He now describes the means for practicing that yoga and the qualified practitioner: "Austerity," etc. A yogi whose mind has been conquered through the austerity of practicing yoga accompanied by the conduct of his own stage of life (āśrama), having settled in a soundless place devoid of the crowding of people for the sake of non-conceptual samādhi, being unattached to internal and external mental constructs, knowing the limbs of yoga, and understanding the reality of the eightfold yoga, remaining indifferent to anything other than himself, should gradually abandon the multitude of conceptual thoughts; the remainder of the sentence is that he should become established in non-conceptual samādhi. || 21 ||
Just as a swan, having cut its bonds— the fruit of meditative concentration— would fly up into the sky without hesitation,
so too the soul, with its bonds severed, forever crosses over saṃsāra. (22)
Just as a lamp, at the time of extinction, goes to its dissolution after burning out, so too the yogi, having burnt away all karmas, goes to his dissolution. || 23 ||

The knower of yoga, having severed the thread [of worldly attachment] with the extremely sharp breath-control (prāṇāyāma) supported by its proper measure and polished by the whetstone of dispassion (vairāgya), is no longer bound. 24.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

He states the fruit of *samādhi* with an illustration: "The snares... (verse 22). Just as a swan, having severed with its own beak the snares of the lotuses of the Mānasa lake that bind its feet, flies up into the sky free from all fear; even so, the yogi—the individual soul (*jīva*)—having completely severed the snares of transmigratory existence with the sharp sword of constant yoga-practice, crosses over *saṃsāra*. Furthermore: "Just as a lamp... (verse 23). Just as a lamp, at the time of extinction, having burnt its own support, wick, and so forth, attains dissolution and peace in its own source; even so, the yogi, having burnt the entire web of karma which constitutes the veil of Brahman alone and obscures his own nature, attains a dissolution that is the negation of anything other than himself. He concludes the meaning of the aforementioned Upanishad: "Prāṇa... (verse 24). The sage who knows the aforementioned yoga, having severed the thread of his own ignorance with the weapon of his own knowledge—which is sharpened by the whetstone of intense dispassion (*vairāgya*) and made exceedingly keen by the means of *prāṇāyāma* and the like, and which has the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) as its basis—is no longer bound by his own ignorance. At the very moment the thread is severed by his own knowledge, the yogi remains as his own Self alone. The word "iti" is for the purpose of removing doubt. The word "Upanishad" signifies the completion of the present Upanishad.
This concise and clear commentary on the Kṣurikā Upaniṣad was written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
It is recorded that this exposition of the Kṣurikā Upaniṣad consists of one hundred and twenty verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Kṣurikopaniṣad, completing the thirty-first [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the ŚrīmadĪśa.
